intro: Happy Enough bubbles along in D major, its tune hopping above a stream of semiquavers. A B♭ slips into the middle and takes the music briefly towards F major.

sections.label: A · A tune above running semiquavers
A · The tune starts again
sections.mNote: The same melody, with a changed final pickup

sections.label: B · B♭ turns towards F major
A · The D-major tune returns

cues.title: Happiness with busy hands
cues.text: The tune rises, drops and catches itself on little rests. Semiquavers keep running underneath, and the left hand sometimes sings back with its own rising phrase. Schumann marks the whole opening piano.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, plate 6016, pp. 8–9, bars 1–8; Ying-Chun Liu’s Mutopia transcription, based on Leichte Stücke (1900). https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=372
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: A B♭ slips in
cues.text: B♭ changes the tune’s direction. Over C in the bass, it belongs to a dominant-seventh chord that leads to F major. The semiquavers continue without a break; the familiar little tune has wandered into a new key.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 9, bars 16–20; C–E–G–B♭ harmony at bar 17 resolves to F major at bar 18.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The bass climbs home
cues.text: The bass climbs by semitones while the melody comes down. A final ritardando brings the running notes to rest on D major.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 9, bars 21–24: chromatic octave bass, ritardando and D-major cadence; pitches checked against the Mutopia transcription.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: G♯ sends the tune round again
transitions.from: A · A tune above running semiquavers
transitions.how: The melody’s G♯ pickup rises to A, and the first eight bars start again. The bass has climbed by semitones to C♯, which carries over into the returning phrase. Schumann writes the repetition out in full.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, pp. 8–9, bars 8–9; G♯ pickup and bass C♯ confirmed in the Mutopia transcription.

transitions.title: A rises to B♭
transitions.to: B · B♭ turns towards F major
transitions.how: This time the pickup is A, and the next melody note is B♭. A C bass carries across the barline beneath it, making a C-seventh chord. The following bar answers in F major, with the semiquavers still flowing.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 9, bars 16–18; bass and chord pitches confirmed in the Mutopia transcription.

transitions.title: D major, then back again
transitions.from: B · B♭ turns towards F major
transitions.how: The bass moves A–D as the tune settles on D, slowed by a ritardando. The printed da capo sends the pianist back to the opening music. Its G♯ pickup and bubbling semiquavers restore the earlier pace.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 9: ritardando, D-major cadence and D.C. The recording’s provisional score alignment follows one eight-bar opening strain on the return.

transitions.title: The C-seventh chord returns
transitions.to: B · B♭ returns, then D major
transitions.how: A rises to B♭ above the C bass again. The same C-seventh chord leads into F major; later, octave bass notes climb by semitones towards the final D-major cadence.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 9, bars 17–24, heard on their second traversal.

composer.epithet: A bookseller’s son who put lovers, masks and arguments into piano music, and made criticism a form of friendship.
facts: Friedrich Wieck, piano; Heinrich Dorn, composition
Co-founded the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik in 1834; edited it until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
composer.background:
Robert Schumann grew up among books in Zwickau. His father August sold and published them, and encouraged his son’s music; Robert read Jean Paul’s novels while learning the piano. The books offered twins, disguises, conversations that wandered away from their subject and returned by an unexpected door. In Papillons, his early set of piano dances, Schumann took up the masked ball at the end of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre. The music changes partners every few bars.

He went to Leipzig to study law in 1828, moved to Heidelberg the following year, and finally persuaded his mother to let him pursue music. Friedrich Wieck undertook to train him as a pianist. Wieck’s young daughter Clara was already performing in public; Robert was the older pupil who had much to catch up on. By 1832, paralysis in his right hand had ended his hopes of becoming a virtuoso. He studied composition with Heinrich Dorn and began building a life at the writing desk.
